name: Call option
definition: A call option is a contract that gives its buyer (holder) the right, but not the obligation, to purchase a specified quantity of an underlying asset or to enter a long futures position at a specified strike price on or before a specified expiration date. The option writer (seller) has the corresponding obligation to sell the underlying if the holder exercises.
intuition: Buying a call is like paying a small fee to lock in a purchase price: if the asset rises above that price you can buy it cheap, and if it doesn't you simply walk away, losing only the fee.
mechanics: The buyer pays a premium to the writer. At expiration a call is worth its intrinsic value max(S - K, 0); before expiration it also carries time value reflecting volatility, time remaining, rates, and dividends. American-style calls may be exercised any time before expiry; European-style only at expiry.
formula: Payoff at expiration (long call) = max(S_T - K, 0); profit = max(S_T - K, 0) - premium, where S_T is the underlying price at expiration and K is the strike price.
failure_modes: Buyers routinely overpay for time value: even a correct directional view loses money if the move is smaller or later than the premium implies (volatility crush, time decay). Sellers face theoretically unlimited loss on uncovered calls.
misconceptions: A call is not 'leveraged stock ownership': the holder has no voting rights or dividends and the contract can expire worthless. Nor is exercise the usual exit; most listed calls are closed by offsetting sale.
example: Buy one XYZ $100 call for a $3 premium (contract = 100 shares, cost $300). If XYZ finishes at $110 at expiration, the call is worth $10 and profit is ($10 - $3) x 100 = $700; if XYZ finishes at or below $100, the loss is the full $300 premium.

name: Put option
definition: A put option is a contract that gives its buyer (holder) the right, but not the obligation, to sell a specified quantity of an underlying asset at a specified strike price on or before a specified expiration date. The put writer has the corresponding obligation to buy the underlying if the holder exercises.
intuition: A put works like an insurance policy on an asset: you pay a premium for the right to sell at a guaranteed price, so a price collapse no longer hurts you beyond the premium.
mechanics: The buyer pays a premium. At expiration a put is worth max(K - S, 0); beforehand it also carries time value. The put holder need not own the underlying and can exercise into a short position. American-style puts may be exercised early; deep in-the-money puts can be rational early-exercise candidates.
formula: Payoff at expiration (long put) = max(K - S_T, 0); profit = max(K - S_T, 0) - premium, where K is the strike price and S_T the underlying price at expiration.
failure_modes: Long puts bleed time value while the underlying moves sideways, and puts bought as 'crash insurance' are chronically expensive because downside implied volatility is usually bid up (skew). Put writers can face losses up to the full strike value if the underlying goes to zero.
misconceptions: A long put is not the same as shorting stock: risk is capped at the premium but the position decays and can expire worthless even if the stock eventually falls. Owning the stock is not required to buy or exercise a put.
example: Buy one XYZ $100 put for a $2 premium. If XYZ falls to $90 by expiration, the put is worth $10 and profit is ($10 - $2) x 100 = $800; if XYZ stays at or above $100, the $200 premium is lost.

name: Moneyness
definition: Moneyness is the position of an underlying asset's price relative to an option's strike price, classifying the option as in-the-money (positive intrinsic value if exercised now), at-the-money (strike equals the current price), or out-of-the-money (zero intrinsic value). It can be measured against spot or against the forward price, and quantified numerically, e.g., by log-moneyness or by the option's delta.
intuition: Moneyness tells you whether an option would be worth anything if it expired right now, and roughly how much 'cushion' it has.
mechanics: Simple moneyness is S/K (or its reciprocal); log-moneyness is ln(F/K); standardized moneyness divides ln(F/K) by sigma*sqrt(T) to express moneyness in standard deviations. Calls are ITM when S > K, puts when S < K. Delta is a common practical proxy for percent moneyness.
formula: Simple moneyness M = F/K (or S/K); standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K) / (sigma*sqrt(T)), where F is the forward price, K the strike, sigma implied volatility, T time to expiry.
failure_modes: Spot-based moneyness misclassifies options when carry is large (high rates or dividends); forward-based (ATMF) classification is then more meaningful. Delta-as-moneyness breaks down for long-dated or high-volatility options where delta diverges from the risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM.
misconceptions: Moneyness is not a statement about profitability of the position — an ITM long option can still be a losing trade if the premium paid exceeds the intrinsic value realized. 'At-the-money' in practice usually means nearest strike, not exact equality.
example: With stock at $100, the $95 call is in-the-money by $5, the $100 call is at-the-money, and the $105 call is out-of-the-money; for puts the relationship is reversed.

name: In-the-money option
definition: An in-the-money (ITM) option is an option with positive intrinsic value: a call whose strike is below the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is above it. Its premium equals intrinsic value plus any remaining time value.
intuition: An ITM option is already 'winning' — exercising it immediately would capture real value, so most of its price moves one-for-one with the underlying.
mechanics: Intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0) for calls and max(K - S, 0) for puts. ITM options have deltas approaching +1 (calls) or -1 (puts) and are the ones exercised (or automatically exercised) at expiration.
formula: Intrinsic value: call = max(S - K, 0); put = max(K - S, 0). Total premium = intrinsic value + time value.
failure_modes: Deep ITM options are illiquid and wide bid-ask spreads can erode the apparent value; holders of ITM American options also carry early-assignment and dividend considerations. Time value can be negative for deep ITM European puts under discounting.
misconceptions: Being ITM does not mean the trade is profitable — an option bought for $8 that is now $5 ITM is still a losing position. ITM short options can be assigned at any time (American style), not only at expiration.
example: With stock at $55, the $50 call is $5 in-the-money; if it trades at $6.20, then $5 is intrinsic value and $1.20 is time value.

name: At-the-money option
definition: An at-the-money (ATM) option is an option whose strike price equals (or is nearest to) the current price of the underlying; in forward terms (ATMF) the strike equals the forward price. An ATM option has no intrinsic value — its entire premium is time value.
intuition: The ATM option is the coin-flip strike: it sits exactly at the boundary between finishing valuable and finishing worthless, which makes it the most sensitive to volatility and time.
mechanics: ATM options have delta near +0.5 (calls) or -0.5 (puts), the highest gamma and theta of the chain, and vega near its maximum. ATM implied volatility is the standard quoting benchmark from which skew/smile adjustments are measured.
failure_modes: Because gamma and theta peak ATM, hedging errors and time-decay estimates are largest here, especially into expiration when tiny price moves flip the option between ITM and OTM (pin risk).
misconceptions: ATM does not mean a 50/50 real-world probability of profit — the buyer must overcome the premium, so the breakeven lies beyond the strike; also, 'ATM spot' and 'ATM forward' strikes differ when rates or dividends are material.
example: With stock at $100.10, the $100 strike is treated as at-the-money; its call might trade at $2.50, entirely time value.

name: Out-of-the-money option
definition: An out-of-the-money (OTM) option is an option with no intrinsic value: a call whose strike is above the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is below it. Its premium consists entirely of time value, and it expires worthless if still OTM at expiration.
intuition: An OTM option is a lottery-like claim: cheap, but it only pays if the underlying moves far enough before time runs out.
mechanics: OTM options have small absolute deltas, lower premiums, and percentage-wise high sensitivity to volatility. The CFTC glossary example: a call with a $400 strike on gold trading at $390 is $10 out-of-the-money.
formula: Intrinsic value = 0; premium = time value only.
failure_modes: Most OTM options expire worthless, so repeated buying of cheap OTM options bleeds capital; conversely, OTM sellers face gap risk — a sudden large move can convert small premium income into large losses. Skew means OTM equity puts are often relatively expensive.
misconceptions: 'Cheap' OTM options are not necessarily good value: their price already embeds the market's implied probability of the required move, and the probability-weighted expected payoff is typically less than the premium after costs.
example: With stock at $100, the $110 call is OTM and might trade at $0.40; unless the stock exceeds $110 at expiration it expires worthless and the buyer loses the $40 per contract.

name: Deep in-the-money option
definition: A deep in-the-money option is an option whose strike is far enough inside the money that its time value is negligible and its price moves almost one-for-one with the underlying (delta near +1 for calls, -1 for puts). 'Deep' is an informal descriptor with no fixed regulatory threshold.
intuition: A deep ITM option behaves almost like a leveraged surrogate for the stock itself, with most of its value being intrinsic.
mechanics: Premium approximates intrinsic value plus minimal time value; gamma, vega, and theta are near zero. Deep ITM American calls on dividend stocks and deep ITM puts are the prime early-exercise candidates because remaining time value can fall below the value of capturing the dividend or strike interest.
failure_modes: Deep ITM strikes are often illiquid with wide bid-ask spreads, so entry/exit costs can exceed the residual time value. Deep ITM European options can trade below intrinsic value due to discounting.
misconceptions: Deep ITM calls are not identical to owning stock: they receive no dividends, and holders must still act (sell or exercise) before expiration; brokers may also auto-exercise them, creating an unintended stock position.
example: With stock at $150, the $100 call is deep ITM and might trade at $50.30 — $50 intrinsic value plus $0.30 time value, with delta near 1.0.

name: Deep out-of-the-money option
definition: A deep out-of-the-money option is an option whose strike is far from the current underlying price, so it has no intrinsic value, a very small delta, and a premium close to zero that consists only of time value. 'Deep' is informal; no fixed threshold defines it.
intuition: A deep OTM option is a cheap tail-risk ticket: it almost always expires worthless but can multiply in value during extreme moves.
mechanics: Price is dominated by the implied probability of a large move (fat tails and skew make these options systematically pricier than lognormal models suggest). Delta-based margin systems treat, e.g., ten deep OTM options with delta 0.20 as two futures-equivalent contracts.
failure_modes: Black-Scholes-style models underprice deep OTM options when return distributions have fat tails — a key lesson of the 1987 crash. Deep OTM quotes are wide and stale, so mark-to-model and end-of-day pricing can be unreliable.
misconceptions: A near-zero price does not mean 'free optionality': the tiny premium reflects a tiny probability-weighted payoff, and repeatedly selling deep OTM options concentrates exposure to rare, severe losses (picking up pennies in front of a steamroller).
example: With the S&P 500 at 5,000, a 30-day 4,000-strike put is deep OTM and may trade for a few cents, yet it is exactly the instrument that pays off in a crash.

name: Option chain
definition: An option chain is a quotation display listing all available option series for a given underlying — typically every strike and expiration for both calls and puts — together with bids, asks, last prices, volume, open interest, and often implied volatility and Greeks.
intuition: The option chain is the menu of every option available on a stock or index, laid out so you can compare strikes and expirations at a glance.
mechanics: Chains are organized by expiration date and strike, with calls and puts shown side by side. Traders read chains to select strikes for strategies, gauge liquidity via volume/open interest and bid-ask width, and compute implied volatilities across the surface.
failure_modes: Displayed quotes can be stale or wide on illiquid series, and last-trade prices may be hours old; using last price instead of current bid/ask misstates fair value and strategy P&L.
misconceptions: High volume on a chain line is not proof of 'smart money' direction — it cannot distinguish opening from closing or buying from selling without trade-level data.
example: Pulling up the SPY option chain for the monthly expiry shows strikes from 400 to 600 in $5 steps, with the at-the-money calls quoted at $3.10 bid / $3.20 ask and open interest of 85,000 contracts.

name: Option series
definition: An option series is the set of option contracts of the same type (all calls or all puts) on the same underlying instrument that share the same expiration date and the same strike (exercise) price — i.e., a single line of an option chain, such as 'XYZ January 100 calls'.
intuition: If the option chain is the menu, a series is one specific dish: one underlying, one expiry, one strike, one side (call or put).
mechanics: All contracts within a series are fungible: any long contract in the series can be offset by selling any contract in the same series. Exchanges list new series as the underlying price moves and as new expiration cycles approach; open interest and volume are reported per series.
failure_modes: Off-the-run series (far dated, deep ITM/OTM) can have zero open interest and no active market maker quotes, making them practically untradable at fair prices.
misconceptions: A 'series' is not a spread or a sequence of trades — it is simply the identifier for all contracts sharing underlying, type, strike, and expiration.
example: The 'AAPL Dec 2026 200 call' series groups every AAPL December 2026 call contract struck at $200; buying and later selling that same series closes the position.

name: Option class
definition: An option class is the set of all option contracts of the same type (calls or puts, but not both) covering the same underlying instrument — for example, all listed calls on XYZ stock across every strike and expiration.
intuition: A class is the whole family of calls (or puts) on one underlying; series are the individual family members.
mechanics: Classes are the unit at which exchanges organize listing, and they aggregate series across strikes and expirations. Position limits, exercise limits, and many spread definitions (e.g., spreads use options 'of the same class') are expressed per class.
failure_modes: Confusing class with series leads to order-entry errors: a spread requires different series within the same class, while offsetting a position requires the identical series.
misconceptions: Option 'class' has nothing to do with share classes of stock (Class A/B shares); it groups option contracts by type and underlying.
example: All listed SPY puts — every strike and every expiration — together form the SPY put class; the Dec 480 put is one series within it.

name: Option writer
definition: An option writer is the party that originates (sells to open) an option contract, receiving the premium and in return accepting the obligation to sell the underlying (call) or buy it (put) if the holder exercises. The CFTC glossary also lists 'option grantor' as a synonym.
intuition: The writer is like an insurance company: it collects the premium up front and must pay out if the insured event (exercise) happens.
mechanics: Writers post margin because their obligations can exceed the premium received. When a holder exercises, the clearing organization assigns the obligation to a writer of that series; writers can close by buying back the same series (offsetting).
failure_modes: Writing naked options exposes the seller to losses many times the premium (unlimited for naked calls); even covered writers face assignment at inconvenient times, e.g., short ITM calls before ex-dividend dates.
misconceptions: Writing an option is not the same as shorting the underlying, and 'most options expire worthless' does not make writing free money — the tail losses on the minority that finish ITM are what the premium compensates.
example: A trader writes one XYZ $50 put and collects $1.50 ($150). If XYZ falls to $45 and the holder exercises, the writer is assigned and must buy 100 shares at $50 — a $350 loss net of premium.

name: Covered call
definition: A covered call is a position long the underlying asset and short a call option on it; the long asset 'covers' the writer's obligation to deliver if the call is exercised. It converts some upside potential into immediate premium income.
intuition: You already own the stock and rent out the upside above the strike: you keep the premium, but if the stock rallies past the strike your shares get called away.
mechanics: For each 100 shares held, the investor sells one call and collects the premium. By put-call parity, a covered call has the same payoff shape as a cash-secured short put at the same strike. Upside is capped at strike + premium; downside is the full stock decline less the premium.
formula: Profit at expiration = (S_T - S_0) + premium - max(S_T - K, 0), per share, where S_0 is the stock purchase price and K the call strike. Max profit = (K - S_0) + premium.
failure_modes: The premium cushions only small declines — a large drop in the stock produces nearly the full stock loss, so it is not downside protection. Repeatedly capping winners while keeping losers can degrade long-run returns (opportunity cost in strong bull markets).
misconceptions: A covered call is not a 'safe income' or low-risk strategy: its payoff is identical to a naked cash-secured short put, which regulators treat as a higher-risk position. Selling a call against stock does not lock in a gain.
example: Own 100 shares of XYZ bought at $48; sell the $50 call for $1.50. If XYZ finishes at $55, shares are called away at $50 for a total profit of ($2.00 + $1.50) x 100 = $350; if XYZ falls to $40, the loss is ($8.00 - $1.50) x 100 = $650.

name: Naked call
definition: A naked (uncovered) call is a short call option position where the writer does not hold the underlying asset or an offsetting position to cover the obligation; the CFTC defines a naked option as the sale of a call or put without holding an equal and opposite position in the underlying instrument.
intuition: You have sold someone the right to buy stock from you at a fixed price without owning the stock — if it soars, you must buy it at the market price to deliver, and there is no ceiling on that price.
mechanics: The writer collects the premium and posts substantial margin. If assigned, the writer must buy the underlying in the open market and deliver it at the strike. Because the underlying price is unbounded, potential loss is theoretically unlimited; brokers restrict naked call writing to high approval levels.
formula: Profit at expiration = premium - max(S_T - K, 0), per share; maximum gain = premium; maximum loss is unbounded.
failure_modes: Gap moves and short squeezes can produce losses far exceeding posted margin before the writer can react; buy-ins after assignment can compound losses. This is the classic structure behind blow-ups from unlimited-risk premium selling.
misconceptions: High win rate does not imply positive expectancy: naked call sellers win the premium often but occasionally lose many multiples of all premiums collected. 'The odds are against exercise' is not a risk control.
example: Write one XYZ $60 call for $2. If XYZ gaps to $90 on takeover news, the writer is assigned and loses ($30 - $2) x 100 = $2,800 on a $200 premium.

name: Cash-secured put
definition: A cash-secured put is a short put option position backed by enough cash in the account to buy the underlying at the strike price if assigned. The writer collects the premium and accepts the obligation to purchase the shares at the strike.
intuition: You get paid a premium to place a limit-buy order: if the stock drops to the strike you buy it (at an effective discount of the premium), and if it doesn't you keep the premium.
mechanics: Sell one put and set aside K x 100 in cash as security. By put-call parity, its payoff equals a covered call at the same strike. Maximum gain is the premium; maximum loss is (K - premium) x 100 if the stock goes to zero. The CBOE S&P 500 PutWrite Index (PUT) benchmarks this strategy systematically.
formula: Profit at expiration = premium - max(K - S_T, 0), per share; breakeven = K - premium.
failure_modes: The 'discount entry' framing fails when the stock falls far below the strike — the writer owns shares well above market. Assignment is likeliest exactly when the stock is collapsing, concentrating losses in bad states.
misconceptions: It is not lower-risk than a covered call — put-call parity makes the two economically identical at the same strike. The cash security covers the purchase obligation, not the market loss on the resulting stock position.
example: Sell one XYZ $45 put for $1.20, securing $4,500 in cash. If XYZ finishes at $47, keep the $120 premium; if assigned at $40, the effective cost basis is $43.80 and the position is already down $380.

name: Protective put
definition: A protective put is a position long the underlying asset plus a long put option on it, which sets a floor on the position's value: losses below the put strike are offset by gains in the put. It is the options-market analogue of buying insurance on a holding.
intuition: You keep all the upside of owning the stock but pay a premium so that, no matter how far it falls, you can always sell at the strike price.
mechanics: Hold (or buy) 100 shares and buy one put, typically at or below the current price. Maximum loss is limited to (S_0 - K) + premium per share; upside remains open, reduced by the premium. By put-call parity, long stock + long put equals a long call plus cash (a fiduciary call).
formula: Profit at expiration = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium, per share; maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium.
failure_modes: Chronic put buying is expensive — downside implied volatility (skew) makes protective puts costly, so persistent hedging can erode returns more than the occasional crash would. Hedging only works to expiration; gaps after expiry are unprotected.
misconceptions: A protective put does not eliminate losses — it caps them at a level that already embeds the premium cost. It is also not 'free insurance' financed by anything; the cost is paid explicitly in premium.
example: Own 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and buy the $48 put for $1. If XYZ collapses to $30, the total loss is capped at ($2 + $1) x 100 = $300 instead of $2,000.

name: Married put
definition: A married put is a protective put in which the underlying shares and the put option are purchased simultaneously as a single package, rather than the put being added to a pre-existing stock holding. The put guarantees a minimum sale price for the shares until expiration.
intuition: It is buying a stock and its insurance policy on the same ticket — you know your maximum possible loss on the combined position from day one.
mechanics: Buy 100 shares and one put at the same time. The payoff is identical to a protective put; the distinction is transactional (simultaneous purchase, which also matters for tax-lot identification in some jurisdictions). By put-call parity the position is equivalent to a long call plus discounted strike cash.
formula: Maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium, per share; profit = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium.
failure_modes: Same as protective puts: the recurring premium drag compounds over time, and protection ends at expiration. Choosing strikes too far OTM leaves a large deductible; too far ITM makes the 'insurance' cost prohibitive.
misconceptions: A married put is not a distinct payoff from a protective put — many texts use the terms interchangeably; the only real difference is the timing of the stock and put purchases. It does not make a falling-stock position safe, only loss-limited.
example: Buy 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and simultaneously buy the $50 put for $2.50. Worst case at expiration is a $250 loss; if XYZ rises to $60 the net gain is ($10 - $2.50) x 100 = $750.

name: Collar
definition: A collar is a position long the underlying asset, long an out-of-the-money put (the floor), and short an out-of-the-money call (the cap) on the same underlying and expiration; the call premium finances part or all of the put. It brackets the position's value between the two strikes.
intuition: You give up the big upside above the call strike to pay for protection against the big downside below the put strike — outcome is 'collared' into a band.
mechanics: Hold 100 shares, buy a put at K1 below the price, sell a call at K2 above it. A 'zero-cost collar' chooses strikes so the call premium equals the put premium. Value at expiration is bounded between K1 and K2 (plus net premium effects).
formula: Value at expiration per share = min(max(S_T, K1), K2) plus/minus net premium; K1 = put strike (floor), K2 = call strike (cap).
failure_modes: The short cap creates regret and assignment risk in strong rallies, and the floor still leaves the band between strikes exposed. Zero-cost construction often forces an uncomfortably tight cap or a distant floor.
misconceptions: A collar is not a free hedge: the put is paid for by surrendered upside, which is a real economic cost. Nor does a zero-cost collar lock in current value — it only bounds the range of outcomes.
example: Own XYZ at $100; buy the $90 put for $2 and sell the $110 call for $2 (zero cost). At expiration the position is worth between $90 and $110 per share no matter where XYZ trades.

name: Bull call spread
definition: A bull call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate rise in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry.
intuition: You buy upside participation but sell away the part above the higher strike to reduce the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.
mechanics: Net debit = premium paid - premium received. Maximum loss is the debit (below the lower strike); maximum gain is (strike width - debit) at or above the higher strike. The CFTC describes the call bull spread as buying the lower-strike (higher-delta) call and selling the higher-strike call.
formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K1 + net debit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
failure_modes: The capped upside badly lags outright call or stock ownership in large rallies; early assignment on the short ITM leg (especially before ex-dividend) can disrupt the spread and create an unintended stock position.
misconceptions: It is not 'free leverage': the reduced cost comes from selling the tail upside, and the probability-weighted expectancy still reflects the market's implied distribution. Limited risk does not mean likely profit.
example: Buy the XYZ $100 call for $4, sell the $105 call for $1.50: debit $2.50. Above $105 the spread is worth $5, a $2.50 gain; below $100 the $250 debit is lost.

name: Bear call spread
definition: A bear call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays below the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (the credit) and maximum loss.
intuition: You sell a call to bet the stock won't rise past your strike, and buy a higher call as a stop-loss so a rally can't hurt you beyond a known amount.
mechanics: Net credit received at entry. Maximum gain = credit if the underlying finishes at or below the short strike; maximum loss = (strike width - credit) above the long strike. The CFTC describes the call bear spread as purchasing the higher-strike call and selling the lower-strike call.
formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K2 - K1) - net credit; breakeven = K1 + net credit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
failure_modes: Frequent small credits are punctuated by losses several times larger; assignment of the short leg near or after expiration can leave a residual stock position (pin risk). Selling calls into strong uptrends repeatedly loses.
misconceptions: A high probability of keeping the credit is not the same as positive expectancy — the loss when wrong is a multiple of the credit. Credit received is not 'income'; it is payment for accepting bounded but real downside.

name: Bull put spread
definition: A bull put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short put at a higher strike and a long put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays above the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (credit) and maximum loss.

name: Bear put spread
definition: A bear put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long put at a higher strike and a short put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate decline in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry.

name: Call debit spread
definition: A call debit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net debit because the lower-strike call costs more than the higher-strike call. failure_modes: The capped upside lags outright calls badly in large rallies; early assignment on the short ITM leg (especially before an ex-dividend date) can leave an unintended stock position and disrupt the spread.
misconceptions: It is not 'free leverage': the lower cost comes from selling the tail upside, and limited risk does not mean likely profit — the debit can still be lost in full.

name: Long straddle
definition: A long straddle is the simultaneous purchase of a call and a put on the same underlying, at the same strike price (typically at-the-money) and the same expiration date. The position profits if the underlying moves far enough in either direction to overcome the combined premium paid.
intuition: You are buying a big move without picking a direction: if the stock swings hard either way one leg pays off, and if it goes nowhere both legs decay.
mechanics: Cost = call premium + put premium; breakevens at expiration are K +/- total premium. The position is long volatility and long gamma, with maximum loss limited to the premium paid if the underlying pins the strike at expiration.
formula: Payoff at expiration = |S_T - K| - (C + P), per share, where C and P are the call and put premiums; breakevens = K + (C + P) and K - (C + P).
failure_modes: The market prices straddles to the expected move, so the buyer loses if realized volatility undershoots implied volatility — the classic post-earnings 'IV crush' loss even when the stock moves. Time decay is steepest for ATM straddles near expiration.
misconceptions: A straddle does not profit from any move, only from moves larger than the premium implies; buying a straddle before a known event means paying an event-inflated premium that typically collapses when the news is out.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $100 call for $3.00 and the $100 put for $2.50 (total $5.50). XYZ must finish above $105.50 or below $94.50 at expiration to profit; a finish at $100 loses the full $550.

name: Short straddle
definition: A short straddle is the simultaneous sale of a call and a put on the same underlying, at the same strike price and the same expiration date, collecting both premiums. It profits most if the underlying finishes exactly at the strike and exposes the seller to unlimited loss above the strike and large loss below it.
intuition: You are selling a big move: you keep both premiums if the stock goes nowhere, but a large swing in either direction costs you point-for-point past the breakevens.
mechanics: Credit = call premium + put premium; breakevens at expiration are K +/- total credit. The position is short volatility and short gamma, with maximum gain equal to the credit and theoretically unlimited risk on the call side. Short straddle losses were a component of Nick Leeson's Barings Bank collapse.
formula: Payoff at expiration = (C + P) - |S_T - K|, per share; max gain = C + P; breakevens = K +/- (C + P).
failure_modes: Gap moves produce losses far exceeding the credit before the seller can react; both legs are naked, so assignment risk, pin risk near expiration, and unlimited upside loss all apply simultaneously.
misconceptions: A high win rate does not make short straddles safe: the occasional large loss dwarfs the accumulated credits. Selling both legs does not 'hedge' the position — the call and put cannot offset each other because only one side can finish in-the-money.
example: With XYZ at $100, sell the $100 call for $3.00 and the $100 put for $2.50 (credit $5.50). If XYZ finishes at $100, keep $550; if XYZ gaps to $115, lose ($15 - $5.50) x 100 = $950.

name: Long strangle
definition: A long strangle is the simultaneous purchase of an out-of-the-money put (lower strike) and an out-of-the-money call (higher strike) on the same underlying with the same expiration date. It is cheaper than a long straddle but requires a larger move in either direction to profit.
intuition: You buy a cheaper ticket on a big move: the strikes are further apart so you pay less, but the stock has to travel further before either leg has value.
mechanics: Cost = OTM call premium + OTM put premium; breakevens at expiration are call strike + total premium and put strike - total premium. Maximum loss is the combined premium if the underlying finishes between the strikes.
formula: Payoff at expiration = max(S_T - K_c, 0) + max(K_p - S_T, 0) - (C + P), where K_c > K_p are the call and put strikes; breakevens = K_c + (C + P) and K_p - (C + P).
failure_modes: Because both legs are OTM, the most likely outcome is a total loss of premium; moves that are large but arrive late still lose to time decay, and event-driven buyers pay inflated implied volatility that collapses after the event.
misconceptions: Cheaper than a straddle does not mean better value: the lower premium reflects a lower probability-weighted payoff, not a bargain.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $105 call for $1.50 and the $95 put for $1.20 (total $2.70). XYZ must finish above $107.70 or below $92.30 to profit; anywhere between $95 and $105 loses the full $270.

definition: A short strangle is the simultaneous sale of an out-of-the-money put (lower strike) and an out-of-the-money call (higher strike) on the same underlying with the same expiration date, collecting both premiums. name: Iron condor
definition: An iron condor is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining an out-of-the-money bull put spread (long lower put, short higher put) and an out-of-the-money bear call spread (short lower call, long higher call), all at four different strikes. The standard ('short') iron condor is entered for a net credit and profits maximally when the underlying finishes between the two short strikes.
intuition: It is a short strangle with the tails cut off: you sell options on both sides of the market but buy further-out options as wings, so your worst case is fixed.
mechanics: Net credit = total premium sold minus premium bought; maximum gain is the credit between the short strikes; maximum loss is the wider wing width minus the credit, realized beyond either long strike. 'Iron' indicates the structure mixes calls and puts, unlike an all-call or all-put condor.
formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = wing width - net credit; breakevens = short put strike - credit and short call strike + credit.
failure_modes: Losses are a multiple of the credit, so a few full-wing losses erase many wins; with four legs, bid-ask slippage and commissions are material, and expiration pin risk on a short strike can leave an unwanted stock position over the weekend.
misconceptions: Defined risk does not mean low risk of ruin: selling far-OTM wings for a 'high probability' condor still concentrates tail exposure. The credit is not income; it is the price of bearing the bounded loss.
example: With XYZ at $100: buy $90 put, sell $95 put, sell $105 call, buy $110 call for a $1.80 net credit. Max gain $180 if XYZ finishes between $95 and $105; max loss $320 beyond either wing.

name: Iron butterfly
definition: An iron butterfly is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining a short straddle at the middle strike (short call and short put at the same strike) with a long out-of-the-money strangle as wings (long lower-strike put, long higher-strike call). Entered for a net credit, it reaches maximum profit when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike.
intuition: It is a short straddle with wings: you sell the at-the-money call and put for a large credit, then buy cheap far-out options to cap the damage if the stock runs.
mechanics: Net credit = premiums sold minus premiums bought; maximum gain is the credit at the middle strike; maximum loss is the wing width minus the credit, realized beyond either long strike. It can be decomposed into a bull put spread and a bear call spread sharing the same short strike.
formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K_wing - K_body) - net credit; breakevens = K_body +/- net credit.
failure_modes: Maximum profit requires the underlying to pin the body strike exactly, a low-probability outcome; the large credit accompanies steep short gamma near expiration, and assignment of an ITM short leg can leave a residual stock position.
misconceptions: The large credit is not an edge over the iron condor — it reflects the narrower, lower-probability profit zone; on a risk-adjusted basis neither structure has an inherent advantage.

name: Long call butterfly
definition: A long call butterfly is a three-strike, same-expiration spread built from calls only: long one call at a lower strike, short two calls at a middle strike, and long one call at a higher strike, with the middle strike equidistant from the wings. Entered for a small net debit, it reaches maximum value when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike.
intuition: You are buying a target: a cheap bet that the stock will land near the middle strike at expiration, with the wings defining your worst case.
mechanics: Net debit = (lower call + upper call) - 2 x middle call; the position is worth zero outside the wings and peaks at the wing width at the body strike. It is a combination of a bull call spread and a bear call spread sharing the short middle strike, and it is short volatility between the wings.
formula: Value at expiration = max(0, min(S_T - K1, K3 - S_T)) when K2 - K1 = K3 - K2; max value = K2 - K1 at S_T = K2; max loss = net debit.
failure_modes: The profit zone is narrow, so the small debit is lost in full most of the time; with three strikes and four contracts, transaction costs consume a large share of the theoretical edge, and short-gamma whipsaw near the body strike close to expiration is severe.
misconceptions: A butterfly's high reward-to-risk ratio is not free money — the maximum payoff is attained only at one exact price, so probability-weighted value, not the peak, determines fairness.
example: Buy the $95 call, sell two $100 calls, buy the $105 call for a $1.00 net debit. Max value $5.00 at $100 (gain $4.00); outside $95-$105 the $100 debit is lost; breakevens at $96 and $104.

name: Broken-wing butterfly
definition: A broken-wing butterfly is a butterfly variant in which the distances between the middle strike and the two wing strikes are unequal — typically the far wing is placed further away (or a strike is skipped), skewing the payoff so that risk is reduced or eliminated on one side at the cost of added exposure on the other.

mechanics: Construction remains 1 long - 2 short - 1 long in the same option type and expiration, but the wing widths differ (e.g., $5 on one side, $10 on the other). The asymmetric strikes shift the peak and can turn the position into a net-credit trade with no loss on one side and an embedded vertical-spread loss on the other.

name: Calendar spread
definition: A calendar spread is the simultaneous sale of an option at a given strike with a nearer expiration and purchase of the same type of option at the same strike with a later expiration, on the same underlying, entered for a net debit. The long calendar profits if the underlying is near the strike when the short leg expires, exploiting the faster time decay of the near-dated option.
intuition: You sell the fast-decaying front month and buy the slow-decaying back month at the same strike, harvesting the difference in decay if the stock stays put.
mechanics: Both legs share the strike; only expirations differ (a 'horizontal' spread). Maximum loss is the net debit; the maximum gain occurs with the underlying at the strike at the first expiration, when the short leg expires worthless while the long leg retains time value. The position is net long vega and net long theta.
formula: Value at first expiration ~ V_long(T2 - T1 remaining) - net debit; exact value requires a model since the long leg still has time value.
failure_modes: A large move in either direction before the first expiration hurts both legs' relative value and can approach the full debit as a loss; a spike in near-term implied volatility (e.g., into earnings) inflates the short leg against the trader. Assignment of the short ITM leg leaves stock-plus-long-option exposure.
misconceptions: A calendar is not a riskless theta harvest — it is a bet on the underlying staying near the strike and on the volatility term structure; losses to the full debit are possible well before the long leg's expiry.
example: With XYZ at $100, sell the 30-day $100 call for $2.50 and buy the 60-day $100 call for $4.00: net debit $1.50. If XYZ is at $100 in 30 days, the short call expires worthless while the long call retains most of its value.

name: Diagonal spread
definition: A diagonal spread is a spread between two calls or two puts on the same underlying that differ in both strike price and expiration date — typically long a longer-dated option at one strike and short a shorter-dated option at a different strike. It combines the directional character of a vertical spread with the time-decay differential of a calendar spread.
intuition: It is a calendar spread tilted with a directional view: the different strikes add a bullish or bearish lean to the front-month decay harvest.
mechanics: Legs differ in strike and expiry, so the payoff depends on both the underlying's level and the term structure of volatility. A common structure, the diagonal call spread (long a longer-dated ITM call, short a near-dated OTM call), behaves like a leveraged covered call; maximum loss is limited to the net debit for the debit variants.
failure_modes: The dual dependence on price and time makes outcomes hard to bound intuitively: big early moves, term-structure shifts, or early assignment of the short leg (especially before ex-dividend dates) can each undermine the position. Rolling the short leg repeatedly converts defined plans into path-dependent outcomes.
misconceptions: A diagonal is not simply a cheaper covered call — unlike stock, the long option decays and can expire worthless, so the 'poor man's covered call' framing hides the long leg's own theta and vega risks.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy the 90-day $90 call for $12 and sell the 30-day $105 call for $1.50: net debit $10.50. If XYZ drifts to $104 by the short leg's expiry, the short call decays while the long call keeps most of its value.

name: Ratio spread
definition: A ratio spread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are sold than bought at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, long one call at a lower strike and short two calls at a higher strike. The extra short option(s) leave part of the position uncovered, giving the spread undefined or large risk beyond the short strikes.
intuition: You finance a directional option purchase by selling two further-out options instead of one — cheap or free to enter, but the second short option is naked and can hurt badly in a big move.
mechanics: Common ratios are 1x2 or 2x3. A 1x2 call ratio spread profits most if the underlying pins the short strike at expiration; beyond the upper breakeven the uncovered short call produces open-ended losses. Often established for a small debit, credit, or zero cost.
formula: 1x2 call ratio payoff = max(S_T - K1, 0) - 2 x max(S_T - K2, 0) - net premium; upper breakeven = 2*K2 - K1 +/- net premium adjustment.
failure_modes: The naked extra short leg converts a 'cheap' spread into an unlimited-risk position on the call side (or strike-sized risk on the put side); gap moves past the short strike realize losses that dwarf the initial outlay, and margin requirements reflect this.
misconceptions: Zero-cost entry does not mean zero risk — the unpaid-for short option is exactly where the risk hides. Ratio spreads are not hedged spreads; they are spreads plus a naked option.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy one $100 call for $4.00 and sell two $105 calls for $2.00 each (zero cost). Max gain $5.00 at $105; above $110 the uncovered short call loses point-for-point without limit.

name: Backspread
definition: A backspread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are bought than sold at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, short one call at a lower strike and long two calls at a higher strike. It is the converse of the ratio spread: the CFTC glossary describes it as a delta-neutral ratio spread in which more options are bought than sold, benefiting from an increase in volatility.
intuition: You sell one near option to finance two further-out options, creating a position that loses a little in a quiet market but pays off disproportionately in a large directional move.
mechanics: Common structure is 1 short x 2 long, often entered near zero net cost. A call backspread has unlimited upside gain beyond the long strikes and a bounded maximum loss when the underlying pins the long strike at expiration; put backspreads mirror this to the downside. The position is net long vega and long gamma.
formula: 1x2 call backspread payoff = 2 x max(S_T - K2, 0) - max(S_T - K1, 0) + net credit; max loss at S_T = K2 equals (K2 - K1) - net credit.
failure_modes: The maximum loss sits exactly at the long strike — the price level traders instinctively anchor to — and slow grind moves lose to time decay; gains require a fast, large move, since a late move arrives after the short leg has already hurt.
misconceptions: A backspread is not 'unlimited profit for free': the zero or credit entry embeds a real loss zone between the strikes, and the position loses in the most common (quiet) scenarios.
example: With XYZ at $100, sell one $100 call for $4.00 and buy two $105 calls for $2.00 each (zero cost). Max loss $500 if XYZ finishes at $105; above $110 the two long calls outrun the short and profit grows without bound.

name: Jade lizard
definition: A jade lizard is a retail-coined, three-leg strategy with one expiration: short an out-of-the-money put and short an out-of-the-money call spread (short a call, long a further OTM call), structured so the total credit collected exceeds the width of the call spread. That sizing condition eliminates upside risk in theory, leaving the naked short put as the only source of loss.
intuition: It is a short strangle with the upside tail capped: you collect premium on both sides, and if the call-spread credit is wide enough, even a runaway rally cannot lose money — only a sell-off can.
mechanics: Construction: sell 1 OTM put at K1, sell 1 OTM call at K2, buy 1 OTM call at K3 (K1 < K2 < K3), same expiry, with credit > (K3 - K2). Maximum gain is the credit if the underlying finishes between K1 and K2; above K3 the call-spread loss is fully offset by the credit; below K1 the short put loses point-for-point down to zero on the stock.
formula: Downside breakeven = K1 - total credit; upside loss = max(0, (K3 - K2) - total credit), which is zero by construction.
failure_modes: The naked put retains full downside exposure to a collapse of the underlying (loss up to the strike times 100 per contract); assignment risk on the short put is real in falling markets, and the 'no upside risk' property can be voided by fees, slippage, or legging in at worse prices.
misconceptions: 'No upside risk' does not mean low risk — the strategy is simply a bullish-skewed short-volatility trade whose entire risk is concentrated on the downside, where equity crashes live.
example: With XYZ at $48: sell the $45 put for $0.90, sell the $52 call for $1.50, buy the $53 call for $1.10 — net credit $1.30 > $1.00 spread width. Max gain $130 between $45 and $52; downside breakeven $43.70.

name: Big lizard
definition: A big lizard is a retail-coined, three-leg strategy with one expiration: short an at-the-money straddle (short call and short put at the same strike) plus long a further out-of-the-money call as an upside wing, sized so the total credit exceeds the width between the straddle strike and the long call. It is the straddle-based analogue of the jade lizard, leaving the naked short put as the only source of loss.
intuition: It is a short straddle with the upside tail capped: you collect a large ATM premium, and if the credit exceeds the call wing's width, a rally cannot lose in theory — only a sell-off can.
mechanics: Construction: sell 1 ATM put and 1 ATM call at strike K, buy 1 OTM call at K2 (K2 > K), same expiry, with total credit > (K2 - K). Maximum gain is the credit if the underlying pins K at expiration; above K2 the call-spread loss is offset by the credit; below K the short put loses point-for-point down to zero on the stock.
formula: Downside breakeven = K - total credit; upside loss = max(0, (K2 - K) - total credit), which is zero by construction.
failure_modes: The naked put side carries full downside exposure in a crash; because the body is a short ATM straddle, the position bleeds badly through even moderate sell-offs, and assignment/pin risk on the ATM strikes near expiration is acute.
misconceptions: 'No upside risk' is a construction property, not a safety feature — the strategy concentrates short-volatility exposure exactly where equity losses cluster, and the large credit is compensation for that.
example: With XYZ at $100: sell the $100 put for $3.00, sell the $100 call for $3.50, buy the $105 call for $2.00 — net credit $4.50 < $5.00 width, so upside is not fully covered; collecting $5.50 instead would remove upside loss. Downside breakeven is $95.50 at a $4.50 credit.

name: Risk reversal
definition: A risk reversal is an options position that is long an out-of-the-money call and short an out-of-the-money put (bullish form), or the reverse (bearish form), on the same underlying with the same expiration; the put premium finances the call. In volatility markets the same term denotes a skew quote: the implied volatility of a given-delta call minus that of the matching put.
intuition: You swap away the downside tail to pay for the upside tail — a synthetic-like way to get leveraged directional exposure for little or no upfront premium.
mechanics: The bullish risk reversal approximates a long forward: it gains as the underlying rises above the call strike and loses below the put strike, where the short put is naked. Dealers quote the 25-delta risk reversal as RR25 = IV(25d call) - IV(25d put), a standard market measure of skew; in equity markets it is usually negative (puts bid over calls).
formula: RR(25-delta) = sigma_call(25d) - sigma_put(25d); position payoff at expiration = max(S_T - K_c, 0) - max(K_p - S_T, 0) - net premium.
failure_modes: The financing short put is naked: a sharp decline produces losses that dwarf the zero-cost entry, and skew means the put sold is often the relatively expensive leg, so the 'free' upside is paid for by selling crash insurance. Early assignment on the short put adds path risk.
misconceptions: A risk reversal is not a directional view with no cost — the cost is the accepted downside tail. Nor is a steep risk-reversal quote proof of informed positioning; it is a relative-pricing (skew) measure, not a forecast.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $105 call for $1.50 and sell the $95 put for $1.50 (zero cost). Above $105 the position gains point-for-point; below $95 it loses point-for-point as if long stock from $95.

name: Synthetic long stock
definition: A synthetic long stock position is a long call and a short put at the same strike and expiration on the same underlying; by put-call parity its payoff replicates owning the underlying outright, gaining or losing point-for-point with the stock from the strike.
intuition: You get the stock's payoff without buying the stock: above the strike you exercise into shares, below it the short put forces the purchase — either way you end up long at the strike.
mechanics: At expiration the combined value equals S_T - K (plus any net premium adjustment), matching a forward purchase at K. The position requires no stock borrow and typically little capital upfront, but the short put carries full downside margin and assignment risk; unlike stock, the synthetic pays no dividends and confers no voting rights.
formula: Value at expiration = max(S_T - K, 0) - max(K - S_T, 0) = S_T - K; initial cost C - P approximates S_0 - PV(K) by put-call parity.
failure_modes: The short put leg is naked and margined, so a sharp decline generates losses and margin calls like leveraged stock ownership; early assignment on the ITM short put (e.g., deep ITM or rate-driven) collapses the synthetic into actual stock before expiration.
misconceptions: A synthetic long is not free leverage: the position carries the full economic exposure of the stock minus dividends, and the apparent cheapness reflects deferred payment of the strike (financing), not a discount.
example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $100 call for $4.50 and sell the $100 put for $4.00 (net debit $0.50). If XYZ finishes at $110, the position is worth $10 for a $9.50 gain — matching 100 shares bought at $100 plus a small financing difference.

name: Synthetic short stock
definition: A synthetic short stock position is a short call and a long put at the same strike and expiration on the same underlying; by put-call parity its payoff replicates being short the underlying, losing or gaining point-for-point as the stock rises or falls from the strike.
intuition: You get the payoff of a short sale without borrowing shares: below the strike the put pays, above it the short call obliges you to sell — either way you are effectively short from the strike.
mechanics: At expiration the combined value equals K - S_T (plus any net premium adjustment), matching a forward sale at K. The structure avoids stock-borrow costs and hard-to-borrow constraints, but the short call is naked with theoretically unlimited risk, and no borrow means no rebate considerations but also margin on the call.
formula: Value at expiration = max(K - S_T, 0) - max(S_T - K, 0) = K - S_T; initial credit P - C approximates PV(K) - S_0 by put-call parity.
failure_modes: The naked short call has unlimited loss in a rally or short squeeze — worse than a stock short in that it cannot be 'covered' by holding shares; assignment on the ITM short call (especially before ex-dividend dates) can force delivery and create borrow needs the structure was meant to avoid.
misconceptions: Avoiding the borrow does not avoid short-seller economics: the options market prices in borrow difficulty through put-call parity (expensive puts / cheap calls), so hard-to-borrow names simply shift the cost into the option prices.
example: With XYZ at $100, sell the $100 call for $4.50 and buy the $100 put for $4.00 (net credit $0.50). If XYZ finishes at $85, the position gains $15, replicating a short sale from $100; above $100 losses are unlimited.

name: Conversion
definition: A conversion is an arbitrage position consisting of long the underlying, long a put, and short a call at the same strike and expiration — long stock plus a synthetic short stock via options, per the CFTC glossary definition. The legs offset into a near-riskless position whose value at expiration equals the strike, so it is traded when the combined price deviates from put-call parity fair value.
intuition: You hold the stock and simultaneously hold its exact mirror image built from options; the two cancel, and any small pricing mismatch between them is the arbitrage profit.
mechanics: Long stock + long put + short call (same K, same expiry) has a constant expiration value of K, independent of the underlying's path. The position is established when the synthetic short (short call + long put) is rich relative to actual stock; profit is the locked-in deviation, financed at prevailing rates until expiration.
formula: Expiration value = S_T + max(K - S_T, 0) - max(S_T - K, 0) = K; fair setup cost approximates PV(K) by put-call parity.
failure_modes: The 'riskless' label ignores execution: legging risk, borrow/assignment on the short call before ex-dividend dates (which strips the stock and breaks the hedge), and financing-cost changes can exceed the thin arbitrage margin. Pin risk at expiration adds uncertainty about residual positions.
misconceptions: Conversions are not free money available to retail: in liquid markets the parity deviation is usually smaller than transaction costs, and early-assignment events turn a flat position into a directional one.
example: Buy 100 XYZ shares at $100, buy the $100 put for $4.00, sell the $100 call for $4.60: net cost $99.40 for a position that will be worth exactly $100 at expiration, locking in $0.60 before carry costs.

name: Reversal conversion
definition: A reversal (reverse conversion) is an arbitrage position consisting of short the underlying, short a put, and long a call at the same strike and expiration — short stock plus a synthetic long stock via options. It is the mirror image of the conversion, traded when the synthetic long is cheap relative to actual stock under put-call parity.
intuition: You are short the stock and long its exact option-built replica; the two cancel into a fixed payoff, monetizing any small mispricing between the stock and its synthetic.
mechanics: Short stock + short put + long call (same K, same expiry) has a constant expiration obligation/value of -K (the position is effectively short the strike). It is established when call-put prices imply a synthetic long cheaper than the actual stock; the position earns the deviation but requires borrowing the shares.
formula: Expiration value = -S_T - max(K - S_T, 0) + max(S_T - K, 0) = -K; fair proceeds approximate PV(K) by put-call parity.
failure_modes: Stock-borrow recall or buy-ins break the hedge and can force unwinds at a loss; assignment on the short put and changes in borrow fees or rates can each consume the thin margin. These are market-maker trades with razor-thin edges.
misconceptions: A reversal is not a directional short: the option legs neutralize the stock exposure, so P&L comes only from pricing deviation and carry, not from the stock falling.
example: Short 100 XYZ shares at $100, sell the $100 put for $4.00, buy the $100 call for $3.40: net proceeds $100.60 against a fixed $100 obligation at expiration, locking in $0.60 before borrow and financing costs.

name: Box spread
definition: A box spread is a four-leg, same-expiration position combining a bull call spread and a bear put spread at the same two strikes — equivalently, long call + short put at the lower strike and short call + long put at the upper strike. Constructed with European-style options it has a constant expiration payoff equal to the strike difference, making it a synthetic zero-coupon loan.
intuition: A box is options-market lending: you pay a fixed price today for a guaranteed fixed payoff at expiration, so the only real variable is the implied interest rate.
mechanics: Because the payoff is fixed at (K2 - K1), the fair price is the present value of that amount; paying less is effectively borrowing, paying more is effectively lending at the implied rate. With American-style index or equity options, early exercise of an ITM leg can break the box and convert it into directional exposure — the source of notorious catastrophic retail losses.
formula: Payoff at expiration (long box) = K2 - K1, constant; fair value = (K2 - K1) * e^(-rT) under put-call parity.
failure_modes: Early assignment on American-style legs destroys the fixed payoff and can produce losses vastly larger than the intended interest-like economics (the infamous 1R0NYMAN case, roughly a 2,000% loss on margin). Execution across four legs also invites slippage that erases the thin rate edge.
misconceptions: A box spread is not 'free money' or riskless yield: with American options it embeds assignment tail risk, and the implied rate is only fair compensation for funding, not an arbitrage gift, once costs are included.
example: A 40-50 box (long 40 call, short 50 call, long 50 put, short 40 put) always pays exactly $10 at expiration; paying $9.80 for it today implies earning roughly the risk-free rate to expiry — unless an American-style leg is assigned early.

name: Put-call parity
definition: Put-call parity is a no-arbitrage identity linking the prices of a European call and a European put at the same strike and expiration to the underlying's forward price: a long call plus a short put replicates a forward contract, so their price difference must equal the discounted difference between the forward price and the strike.
intuition: Whether the stock finishes above or below the strike, one of the two options is exercised and you end up buying at the strike — exactly like a forward — so the two packages must cost the same today.
mechanics: Formally C - P = D x (F - K), or in spot terms C - P = S - PV(K) for non-dividend stocks, extended to C - P = S - PV(K) - PV(dividends) when dividends are paid. The identity is model-free (static replication) and underlies synthetic positions, conversions/reversals, and the equivalence of covered calls to cash-secured puts; violations beyond transaction costs imply arbitrage.
formula: C - P = S_0 - K*e^(-rT) - PV(dividends); equivalently C + PV(K) = P + S_0 (fiduciary call = married put).
failure_modes: Parity holds exactly only for European options in frictionless markets; American early-exercise rights, dividends, borrow costs, and wide bid-ask spreads create bands within which deviations persist without being exploitable. During market stress, financing and borrow constraints widen these bands dramatically.
misconceptions: Parity is not a pricing model that predicts option values — it is a consistency condition among prices that already exist. Nor does it require assumptions about volatility or the underlying's distribution.
example: With XYZ at $100, one-year $100-strike European call at $8.00, and the risk-free rate near zero, parity implies the $100 put should trade near $8.00 too; if it traded at $5.00, a conversion would lock in the $3.00 discrepancy.

name: Early exercise
definition: Early exercise is the exercise of an American-style option before its expiration date. It is rational only in specific circumstances — principally calls on a stock just before an ex-dividend date (to capture the dividend) and deep in-the-money puts (to capture the strike's interest value) — because exercising otherwise destroys the option's remaining time value.
intuition: Exercising early is like tearing up an insurance policy to claim it today: you get the intrinsic value but throw away the remaining time value, so it pays only when something specific (a dividend, interest on the strike) exceeds that sacrifice.
mechanics: An American call on a non-dividend stock should never be exercised early (Merton's result): selling the option always yields at least as much. Before an ex-dividend date, exercising an ITM call is optimal when the dividend exceeds the remaining time value; deep ITM puts can be optimal to exercise early because the strike cash earns interest immediately. Writers face early assignment randomly through the OCC's allocation process.
formula: Rule of thumb: early-exercise an ITM call before ex-date only if dividend > time value of the call; never early-exercise a call on a non-dividend-paying stock.
failure_modes: Retail holders routinely forfeit time value by exercising when selling would pay more; writers who ignore dividend calendars get assigned at the worst times and find their 'covered' position stripped of stock the day before ex-dividend.
misconceptions: Early exercise is not generally 'taking profit early' — it usually leaves money on the table versus selling the option. The blanket rule 'never exercise early' is also wrong: dividends and deep ITM puts create legitimate exceptions.
example: XYZ trades at $55 and goes ex-dividend tomorrow for $1.00; the $50 call trades at $5.10 ($5.00 intrinsic + $0.10 time value). Since the $1.00 dividend exceeds the $0.10 time value, exercising today to hold the stock over the ex-date is rational.

name: Pin risk
definition: Pin risk is the uncertainty faced by an option writer when the underlying closes at or very near the short option's strike at expiration: the writer cannot predict whether the option will be exercised, so they cannot determine whether they will wake up after expiration with an unwanted long or short stock position.
intuition: The stock finishes a cent away from your strike on expiration Friday, and you do not know whether you own 1,000 shares on Monday — that unknowable weekend exposure is pin risk.
mechanics: Holders' exercise decisions depend on their own transaction costs, so slightly ITM options may go unexercised and slightly OTM or ATM options are occasionally exercised. Under OCC exercise-by-exception, options $0.01 or more ITM are auto-exercised absent contrary instructions, but exceptions and after-hours news leave the writer guessing. Spread traders face the amplified version: one leg assigned and the other not converts a defined-risk spread into naked stock over the weekend.
failure_modes: The standard failure is the Monday-morning gap: a short spread pinned at the short strike Friday leaves the trader long or short the underlying after partial assignment, and a weekend gap converts a 'defined-risk' trade into a loss far exceeding the spread width.
misconceptions: Closing near the strike does not mean the option 'expires worthless safely' — ATM and even slightly OTM options are sometimes exercised deliberately. Letting defined-risk spreads expire rather than closing them is the classic way pin risk ambushes retail accounts.
example: A trader is short the $50 put; XYZ closes Friday at $49.97. Only some holders exercise, so instead of being flat, the trader is long an unexpected 4,900 shares Monday and must cover a gap at the open.

name: Assignment risk
definition: Assignment risk is the possibility that the writer of an American-style option is assigned an exercise notice at any time before expiration, obliging them to sell the underlying at the strike (call) or buy it at the strike (put). Assignment is most likely when a short option is in-the-money with little remaining time value, especially calls just before an ex-dividend date and deep ITM puts.
intuition: When you sell an option, someone else holds the trigger: they can pull it early, and you must then deliver or buy shares at the strike whether or not the timing suits you.
mechanics: When a holder exercises, OCC randomly assigns the notice to a clearing member with a short position in that series, which in turn assigns a customer (randomly or first-in-first-out, by firm policy). Assignment creates a stock position and cash obligation the writer must fund; for spread holders, assignment of one leg can leave residual directional exposure and margin calls.
failure_modes: Assignment strikes when the position is hardest to manage: ex-dividend mornings strip covered-call writers of their shares just before the payout, and spread traders discover over a weekend that one leg was exercised, converting defined risk into naked stock exposure plus a margin call.
misconceptions: Assignment is not a penalty or an error — it is the obligation the writer was paid to accept, and it can happen any day, not just at expiration. Avoiding assignment entirely requires closing the short option, not merely monitoring it.
example: A trader short the $50 covered call watches XYZ rally to $58 the week before a $0.80 ex-dividend date; the holder exercises early to capture the dividend, and the writer is assigned, losing the shares at $50 and forgoing the expected continued upside.

name: Dividend risk
definition: Dividend risk is the risk to a short call writer that the call is exercised early, just before the underlying's ex-dividend date, because the holder wants to own the stock in time to receive the dividend. It also refers more broadly to the effect of expected dividends on option prices — calls are cheaper and puts richer the larger the anticipated dividend.
intuition: Options do not pay dividends, so the day before a payout, an in-the-money call holder may grab the stock (and its dividend) by exercising — leaving you, the writer, assigned and delivering shares plus the dividend's value.
mechanics: A call holder is entitled to the dividend only if they exercise before the ex-dividend date; per OCC/OIC guidance, early exercise is rational when the dividend exceeds the call's remaining time value, so assignment probability on short ITM calls rises into ex-dates. Assigned writers must deliver stock and may be notified only after the ex-date, making the exposure invisible until it has happened.
formula: Early-exercise trigger (rule of thumb): dividend > call time value remaining; with multiple dividends remaining, compare against time value of the earliest profitable exercise.
failure_modes: Covered-call and spread writers who ignore dividend calendars are assigned at the worst moment, losing stock before the dividend and breaking hedges; deep ITM short call legs of spreads are prime targets, and the residual long leg plus new short stock changes the account's risk profile overnight.
misconceptions: Dividends are not 'extra return' for option holders — option strike prices are not adjusted for ordinary dividends, so the stock's ex-date drop mechanically transfers value from calls to puts, and only exercise before the ex-date captures the payment.

name: Exercise-by-exception
definition: Exercise-by-exception is the OCC's administrative procedure under which expiring options that are in-the-money by a specified threshold ($0.01 per contract for equity and index options) are automatically exercised for clearing members unless contrary instructions are submitted. It is a default mechanism between OCC and its clearing members, not a substitute for customer exercise instructions.
intuition: At expiration the clearinghouse assumes you want your in-the-money options exercised — unless you or your broker say otherwise — so worthless-by-a-cent positions do not silently evaporate and valuable ones are not accidentally abandoned.
mechanics: After the close on expiration day, OCC exercises options meeting the threshold based on the underlying's official closing price, absent contrary instructions from the clearing member. Brokers may apply different (often higher) thresholds for retail accounts, and holders can always instruct contrary exercise — including exercising an option that is not ITM by the threshold.
formula: Threshold: exercise if (closing price - strike) >= $0.01 for calls, or (strike - closing price) >= $0.01 for puts (equity/index).
failure_modes: Holders who assume only clearly ITM options are exercised get surprised: after-hours news can move the underlying past the threshold after they stopped paying attention, and writers of slightly ITM shorts can be assigned while holders of slightly OTM longs can still choose to exercise. The result is unwanted stock positions discovered after expiration.
misconceptions: Exercise-by-exception is not truly 'automatic': OCC stresses that contrary instructions are always permitted, so neither writers nor holders can rely on the threshold as a guarantee of what will happen to a pinned strike.
example: XYZ closes expiration Friday at $100.02; the $100 calls are $0.02 ITM and are auto-exercised by exception, so writers of those calls are assigned even though the option looked nearly worthless at 3:59 pm.

name: Delta
definition: Delta is the first-order sensitivity of an option's price to a small change in the underlying's price: the partial derivative of option value with respect to the underlying price. A call delta ranges from 0 to +1 and a put delta from -1 to 0; the CFTC defines it as the expected change in an option's price per one-unit change in the underlying's price.
intuition: Delta tells you how many shares of stock your option currently behaves like: a 0.50-delta call gains about fifty cents when the stock rises a dollar.
mechanics: In Black-Scholes, call delta = N(d1) and put delta = N(d1) - 1 (for a non-dividend stock). Delta is the hedge ratio for delta-hedging, is used as a rough proxy for the risk-neutral probability of finishing in-the-money, and aggregates linearly across a portfolio. Delta itself changes as the underlying moves, which is what gamma measures.
formula: Delta = dV/dS; Black-Scholes: call delta = N(d1), put delta = -N(-d1) = N(d1) - 1.
failure_modes: Delta hedging is exact only for infinitesimal moves with all other inputs frozen; gaps, volatility changes, and time decay make realized hedge P&L diverge. The delta-as-probability proxy is only an approximation (it conflates N(d1) with the N(d2) exercise probability) and degrades for long-dated or high-volatility options.
misconceptions: Delta is not the true real-world probability of finishing ITM — it is a sensitivity under the risk-neutral pricing framework. Nor is a delta-hedged position riskless: it remains exposed to gamma, vega, and theta.
example: An XYZ $100 call with delta 0.60 gains roughly $0.60 when XYZ rises from $100 to $101; a trader long 10 such calls can delta-hedge by shorting 600 shares.

name: Gamma
definition: Gamma is the second-order sensitivity of an option's price to the underlying's price — the rate of change of delta per unit change in the underlying. Long options have positive gamma and short options negative gamma; gamma peaks for at-the-money options near expiration.
intuition: Gamma is the accelerator pedal of your delta: the higher the gamma, the faster your position turns more long as the stock rises and more short as it falls.
mechanics: Gamma = d(delta)/dS = d2V/dS2; identical for calls and puts at the same strike in Black-Scholes. It measures the convexity of the option's value and the cost of re-hedging a delta-neutral book: long-gamma positions gain from realized volatility and pay theta; short-gamma positions collect theta and lose to realized volatility.
formula: Gamma = d2V/dS2; Black-Scholes: Gamma = N'(d1) / (S * sigma * sqrt(T)).
failure_modes: Near expiration, ATM gamma explodes, so hedges that looked adequate become useless within hours and small price jumps force large re-hedges; short-gamma books are exactly where gap moves inflict unbounded damage, and gamma estimates are model-dependent.
misconceptions: Long gamma does not mean 'profits from any move' — it profits only when realized volatility exceeds the implied volatility paid for via theta. Gamma is also not a standalone position: it is inseparable from the theta cost that funds it.
example: A $100-strike call with delta 0.50 and gamma 0.08 sees its delta rise to about 0.58 if the stock rises $1; a short option with gamma -0.08 must buy back 8 deltas of hedge after that same move.

name: Theta
definition: Theta is the sensitivity of an option's price to the passage of time, holding all other inputs constant — conventionally reported as the (typically negative) change in option value per day. Long options usually have negative theta and short options positive theta; theta is largest in magnitude for at-the-money options near expiration.
intuition: Theta is the daily rent you pay to own an option: every day that passes with the stock unmoved, a little more of the premium evaporates.
mechanics: Theta = -dV/d(tau) by practitioner convention, where tau is time to expiry. Time decay is non-linear, accelerating into expiration for ATM options, and it is the mirror image of gamma: long-gamma positions pay theta and short-gamma positions collect it. Deep ITM European puts can have positive theta because of discounting effects.
formula: Theta = -dV/d(tau); Black-Scholes call theta = -(S*N'(d1)*sigma)/(2*sqrt(T)) - r*K*e^(-rT)*N(d2).
failure_modes: Theta is a model value assuming constant implied volatility and price — real decay is lumpy (weekends, events, IV changes), so daily theta estimates routinely misstate actual overnight P&L. Strategies sold as 'theta harvesting' silently assume realized volatility stays below implied.
misconceptions: Theta is not guaranteed income for sellers: it is compensation for bearing gamma risk, and the two are linked by the pricing PDE. Buyers likewise do not 'lose theta' on weekends in a simple daily pro-rata way — models price decay continuously while markets price it in discrete jumps.
example: A $100-strike call trading at $3.00 with theta -0.05 loses about $0.05 overnight if price and implied volatility are unchanged; after a quiet week it would be worth roughly $2.65, all else equal.
